claims.text: Local chemical short-range order in multi-component concentrated alloys generates spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy.
Shear-fault-energy fluctuations act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Local chemical order raises the activation or unpinning barriers governing dislocation motion.
Fluctuations in shear-fault energy are a governing source of strength in complex concentrated alloys.
Short-range order modifies dislocation glide behavior and the selection of slip, faulting, and twinning pathways.
Short-range order can intensify planar slip.
Short-range order can modify twinning activity.
A homogenized near-equiatomic CrCoNi or NiCoCr alloy can serve as a relatively random state lacking pronounced short-range order.
Heat treatment can promote L11- or L12-type short-range-order motifs in nanoscale clusters.
Low-temperature mechanical pre-straining can be used to promote short-range order.
Nanoscale short-range-ordered clusters create local variations in the planar-fault-energy landscape.
Enhancing short-range order will increase yield strength relative to a homogenized baseline.
Enhancing short-range order will increase the work-hardening rate or capacity.
Enhancing short-range order will produce distinct dislocation-slip patterns, including more planar slip.
Enhancing short-range order will reduce fault propagation or the propensity for faulting.
The proposed effect should govern behavior from room temperature to cryogenic temperatures when dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates.
The comparison should hold grain size, texture, overall composition, strain rate, and temperature constant.
The hypothesis may cease to apply when phase transformations or diffusion-driven mechanisms dominate at very high temperatures or extreme strain rates.
Solid-solution and lattice-distortion strengthening may contribute concurrently and obscure the magnitude attributable to short-range order.

Failure of the enhanced-SRO samples to show statistically significant changes in strength, work hardening, or slip patterns relative to the controlled baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of SRO-induced fault-energy fluctuations.
